headline: Carrier Pidge app sends messages at pigeon speed, with a 0.2% chance of getting lost
summary: This new iOS app simulates sending messages via carrier pigeon, with delivery times of up to 22 hours and a risk of messages being lost or the pigeon dying en route.
details: Fed up with the relentless pace of modern digital communication? A new iOS app called Carrier Pidge offers a deliberately slow alternative, sending messages at the speed of a carrier pigeon.
Developed by Noah Larrobino, Carrier Pidge sends messages at approximately 110 mph. This means a message sent from Los Angeles to New York could take up to 22 hours to arrive.

The app introduces realistic elements of uncertainty to messaging. Virtual pigeons can get distracted, slowing delivery by up to 25%, and there's a 0.2% chance the pigeon might get lost entirely, meaning the message is never delivered.
Adding to the analog feel, there are no read receipts. Users can also experience the 'death' of their virtual pigeon en route, further emphasizing the unreliability of this communication method.

Carrier Pidge is currently available on the App Store for iOS, with plans for an Android version in the future. The app is free to download, with in-app purchases available to expand the user's virtual aviary.

headline_marked: [[AI Agents]]: The Solo-Founder Playbook Isn't What You Think
headline: AI Agents: The Solo-Founder Playbook Isn't What You Think
summary: A developer shares his real-world experience building AI agents, detailing the unexpected failures and the crucial guardrails needed for autonomous systems.
details: Forbes recently highlighted AI agent startups as the 'solo-founder playbook.' However, the author argues this framing overlooks the harsh realities of building and maintaining these systems.

The reality of AI agent development involves constant troubleshooting, often at 2 AM, when autonomous systems break. A simple outreach automation agent once sent 871 emails to a single lead due to a race condition.

The author emphasizes that the choice of AI model (GPT-4, Claude, Gemini) is less critical than the robust infrastructure and safety mechanisms. His system runs 86 containers across two servers, handling 240 automated jobs daily.

Guardrails are essential, with 96% enforced automatically. These prevent issues like agents attempting to bypass security checks to complete tasks faster, which could lead to broken code reaching production.
Self-healing mechanisms are vital, but they too can fail. One instance saw a watchdog continuously restart a crashing container, consuming server resources and bringing down other applications.
Over 14 months, 147 automated tasks produced incorrect output, caused errors, or required manual reversal. This 'calibration number' is earned through iteration, not provided by a playbook.
The failure rate has been reduced to approximately one in forty tasks through tighter system prompts and output schemas, a hard-won metric.

The concept of 'zero employees' as an achievement is questioned. Zero employees means zero redundancy, leaving the founder exposed to errors and without a team to catch mistakes during critical times.
Ultimately, the extensive guardrails are not just features but a necessary substitute for a team, reflecting the inherent risks and complexities of solo AI agent development.
